statement: An inventory of information and associated assets, including hardware, software, cloud services and data stores, is kept with a named owner for every entry. It is updated whenever assets are added, changed or retired, and reconciled with live sources such as the cloud console and the device management tool on a defined cycle. The inventory and the reconciliation records are the proof.
why_asked: Assets nobody knows about are never patched, monitored or protected, and unowned assets have no one to answer for them. The inventory is also the base for most other controls.
how_to_ask: Ask to see the inventory itself, not the policy about it. Check that it covers cloud and software as well as laptops, and that owners are people. Pick a few live assets and look for them in the list. Example probe: "Show me a cloud resource created last month and where it appears in the inventory."
question: Does your organization keep a current inventory of information and associated assets, with an owner assigned to each one?
expected_evidence: Asset inventory export with owner column; the inventory update procedure; cloud console or device management export used for reconciliation; most recent reconciliation record. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: The inventory covers hardware, software, cloud services and data stores in scope. Every entry has a named owner. A recent reconciliation shows live assets match the list and gaps were fixed.
test: Sample live assets from the cloud console or device management tool and look each one up in the inventory. Check that every sampled entry has an owner and that the inventory was updated within its defined review cycle. Pass if all sampled live assets are listed with an owner and the update is on time.
baseline_risk: Unknown or unowned assets go unpatched and unmonitored, and incidents cannot be traced to a responsible person.

statement: Written rules for acceptable and prohibited use of information and assets are set, and handling of information at each classification level is documented, including storage, sharing, transport and disposal. Users acknowledge the rules when they join and again on a defined cycle. Signed acknowledgement records are the proof.
why_asked: Without written rules, staff cannot be held to a standard and misuse is hard to act on. Acknowledgements show users were told the rules.
how_to_ask: Ask for the acceptable use policy and the handling procedure, then ask how staff accept them. Check that handling differs by classification level. Example probe: "How do you know a contractor who joined in the spring has accepted the acceptable use rules?"
question: Does your organization set rules for acceptable use and handling of information that users acknowledge?
expected_evidence: Acceptable use policy; information handling procedure by classification level; user acknowledgement records or onboarding sign-offs; the policy approval record. Cover the last two review cycles.
good_looks_like: A policy states permitted and prohibited uses. A handling procedure covers each classification level. Acknowledgements exist for current staff and new joiners, and are repeated on the defined cycle.
test: Read the policy and the handling procedure for permitted and prohibited uses and each classification level. Sample current users and new joiners and check each has a recorded acknowledgement. Pass if both documents are approved and all sampled users have acknowledged the current version.
baseline_risk: Staff mishandle or misuse information and assets with no agreed standard to enforce.

statement: All organizational assets, such as devices, badges, tokens and documents, are returned by personnel and external parties when they leave or change role, contract or agreement. The leaver or role-change checklist requires return and checks each returned item against the asset inventory. Completed checklists are the proof.
why_asked: Unreturned laptops, tokens and badges leave data and access in the hands of people who no longer have a right to them.
how_to_ask: Ask how a leaver's equipment is collected and who signs it off. Ask for completed checklists, not the template. Example probe: "Take the last contractor who left. Which items did they hold and where is the record that each came back?"
question: Does your organization make sure personnel and external parties return all organizational assets when they leave or change role, contract or agreement?
expected_evidence: Leaver and role-change procedure with asset return step; completed leaver checklists; asset inventory entries updated on return; list of leavers for the period. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: The procedure requires return of all asset types, including for contractors. Each checklist shows items returned and matched to the inventory. Missing items are chased and recorded.
test: Sample leavers and role changes from the audit period and open each completed checklist. Check that every asset recorded against the person in the inventory is shown as returned or accounted for. Pass if all sampled leavers have a completed checklist reconciled to the inventory.
baseline_risk: Departing people keep devices, tokens and documents, exposing data and access after they leave.

statement: An information classification scheme sets levels and criteria for assigning them, based on confidentiality, integrity, availability and stakeholder needs. A level is assigned to each information asset in the inventory and reviewed when use or sensitivity changes. The scheme and the classified inventory are the proof.
why_asked: Without classification, protection is applied evenly or by guesswork, so sensitive data is under-protected or everything is over-protected at high cost.
how_to_ask: Ask for the scheme and then the inventory with the classification column filled in. Check that the criteria let two people reach the same level. Example probe: "Which level would customer contracts get, and who decided?"
question: Does your organization classify information by its confidentiality, integrity, availability and stakeholder needs using a defined scheme?
expected_evidence: Information classification scheme with level definitions and criteria; asset inventory showing classification per asset; classification review records. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: The scheme defines levels with clear criteria that weigh secrecy, accuracy and uptime and stakeholder needs. Information assets in the inventory carry a level. Owners review levels when things change.
test: Read the scheme for levels and assignment criteria covering confidentiality, integrity, availability and stakeholder needs. Sample information assets in the inventory and check each has a classification consistent with the criteria. Pass if the scheme is approved and all sampled assets are classified.
baseline_risk: Sensitive information is not recognized, so it gets the same weak protection as public data.

statement: The marking for each classification level on documents, systems and media is defined, and labels are applied as the procedure requires, supported by tool settings where available. The labelling procedure and a sample of labelled items are the proof.
why_asked: Labels tell people and tools how to handle information. Without them, the classification scheme exists only on paper.
how_to_ask: Ask for the labelling procedure, then ask to see real labelled documents and the tool settings that apply labels. Example probe: "Open a confidential document from last month. Where is the label and was it applied by a person or automatically?"
question: Does your organization label information in line with its classification scheme?
expected_evidence: Labelling procedure; classification scheme with marking rules; sample labelled documents, systems and media; sensitivity label or tagging tool configuration export. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: The procedure states the marking for each level on documents, systems and media. Tools apply or prompt for labels. Sampled items carry labels that match the procedure.
test: Sample documents, records and media from the audit period and check each carries the label the procedure requires for its level. Review the labelling tool configuration. Pass if all sampled items are labelled as the procedure states.
baseline_risk: Staff cannot tell how sensitive an item is, so it is shared or stored incorrectly.

statement: Rules for every channel used to transfer information, such as email, file sharing, removable media, courier and verbal, are set, stating the protection each sensitivity level needs. Transfers with external parties are covered by agreements with security terms, and technical settings on the main channels enforce the rules. Rules, agreements and configuration exports are the proof.
why_asked: Information leaks most often in transit or when handed to a third party. Rules with no technical enforcement or agreements rely on goodwill.
how_to_ask: Ask which channels staff use to send sensitive information outside, then ask for the rule, the agreement and the setting for each main one. Example probe: "How is a customer file sent to a supplier, and what stops someone sending it by personal email instead?"
question: Does your organization set rules, agreements and technical settings for each channel used to transfer information, matched to its sensitivity?
expected_evidence: Information transfer policy or procedure; sample agreements with external parties containing security terms; email transport protection and external sharing settings export; list of approved transfer channels. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: Each channel in use has a rule linked to classification. External transfers sit under agreements with security terms. Settings on the main channels, such as encrypted mail transport and limits on external sharing, enforce the rules.
test: Read the transfer rules and check each channel in use is covered. Sample external parties and check each has an agreement with security terms. Inspect configuration exports for the main channels. Pass if all channels are covered, all sampled agreements have security terms and settings match the rules.
baseline_risk: Sensitive information is sent over unprotected channels or to third parties with no obligation to protect it.

statement: A records retention schedule defines record types, retention periods and storage requirements based on legal and contractual needs. Stored records are protected from loss, destruction, falsification and unauthorized access or release for the whole retention period, using access limits, immutability or backups. The schedule and storage settings are the proof.
why_asked: Records that are lost, altered or deleted early can leave the organization unable to prove compliance or defend a claim.
how_to_ask: Ask for the retention schedule, then pick two or three record types and ask where they live and who can change or delete them. Example probe: "Who can delete a signed customer contract from the repository today, and would anyone notice?"
question: Does your organization retain records for the required periods while protecting them from loss, destruction, falsification and unauthorized access?
expected_evidence: Records retention schedule; compliance or legal register supporting the periods; storage and access settings for sampled record types; backup configuration and restore records. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: The schedule lists record types, retention periods, storage locations and the legal or contractual basis. Sampled record types are protected against deletion and tampering through access limits, immutability or backups.
test: Read the schedule for record types, periods and storage requirements tied to legal and contractual needs. Sample record types and inspect storage settings for deletion and tamper protection through the retention period. Pass if the schedule is complete and all sampled record types are protected.
baseline_risk: Required records are lost or altered, which leaves the organization unable to prove what happened or meet legal duties.

statement: The point at which information must be deleted from systems, devices and media once it is no longer needed, and the method of deletion, are defined. Information is deleted on that schedule, using automated jobs or manual steps, and deletion logs or supplier confirmations are kept as proof.
why_asked: Information kept past its purpose adds breach exposure and legal risk. Deletion that is not proven cannot be relied on.
how_to_ask: Ask for the deletion rule, then ask for the latest deletion log or job output. Include data held by suppliers. Example probe: "Show me what was deleted last quarter and who confirmed a supplier deleted its copy."
question: Does your organization delete information that is no longer needed from systems, devices and media by a defined method with proof?
expected_evidence: Retention and deletion procedure; deletion method standard; automated deletion job output and deletion logs; supplier deletion confirmations; the records retention schedule. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: The procedure states triggers and methods for deletion across systems, devices and media. Logs or confirmations show deletions happened on schedule, including at suppliers.
test: Read the procedure for deletion triggers and methods. Sample items due for deletion in the audit period and trace each to a deletion log, job record or supplier confirmation. Pass if all sampled items were deleted on schedule with proof on file.
baseline_risk: Unneeded information accumulates, enlarging the impact of any breach and breaching retention duties.

statement: The data that must be masked, pseudonymized or anonymized, the contexts in which this applies and the technique to use are defined. Masking is applied in non-production environments, support screens and reports as the standard requires. The standard and samples of masked data are the proof.
why_asked: Real personal or sensitive data in test environments and support tools is widely exposed to people who do not need it.
how_to_ask: Ask which data is masked and where. Ask to see a test dataset and a support screen. Example probe: "Show me a record in the test system and tell me whether the names and ID numbers are real."
question: Does your organization mask, pseudonymize or anonymize data where its rules and applicable law require?
expected_evidence: Data masking standard or policy; list of masked data types and contexts; sample non-production datasets; screenshots of support screens and reports; masking tool configuration. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: The standard names data types, contexts and techniques. Non-production data, support screens and reports show masking applied as required.
test: Read the standard for data types, contexts and techniques. Sample non-production datasets, support screens and reports and check masking is applied as stated. Pass if all sampled items show masking that matches the standard.
baseline_risk: Sensitive data is exposed to developers, testers and support staff who do not need it.
applicability: Applies if the organization holds personal or other sensitive data in non-production environments, support tools or reports.

statement: The sensitive information that could leak and the channels it could leak through, such as email, uploads, removable media and printing, are identified. Leakage prevention measures are configured on those channels, and alerts are reviewed and acted on. Configuration exports and the alert review log are the proof.
why_asked: Policy alone does not stop a user sending sensitive files out. Alerts nobody reads give a false sense of control.
how_to_ask: Ask what sensitive data is covered and which channels are monitored or blocked. Then ask for the alert queue and what was done with the last alerts. Example probe: "Walk me through the last leakage alert, who looked at it and what happened next."
question: Does your organization prevent sensitive information from leaking through the channels it could leak through, acting on alerts?
expected_evidence: List of sensitive information and leakage channels; leakage prevention rule and endpoint configuration export; upload and removable media blocking settings; alert log with review and action records; related incident records. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: The sensitive data and channels are documented. Prevention rules are active on those channels. Alerts are reviewed on a regular basis and lead to recorded actions.
test: Compare the list of channels with the configuration export and check prevention is set on each. Sample alerts from the audit period and check each was reviewed and acted on. Pass if all identified channels are covered and all sampled alerts have a recorded review.
baseline_risk: Sensitive information leaves the organization unnoticed through unmonitored channels.

statement: Storage media are managed through acquisition, use, transport, storage and disposal according to classification and handling rules. Technical controls restrict or encrypt removable media on endpoints as the procedure requires. The media handling procedure and endpoint policy settings are the proof.
why_asked: Unencrypted USB drives and tapes are easily lost or stolen and carry data with them.
how_to_ask: Ask for the media procedure, then ask what happens when someone plugs in a USB drive. Example probe: "Insert a personal USB drive on a standard laptop. What does the device do?"
question: Does your organization manage storage media from acquisition to disposal in line with classification and handling rules?
expected_evidence: Media handling procedure; endpoint policy export for removable media; list of approved media and transport rules; media register. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: The procedure covers each media stage and classification. Endpoint settings block or encrypt removable media. Media in use is tracked.
test: Read the procedure for coverage of each media stage by classification. Inspect endpoint policy settings for removable media and test a sample of endpoints. Pass if the procedure covers all stages and all sampled endpoints restrict or encrypt removable media as stated.
baseline_risk: Data on lost or stolen media is exposed because media was neither tracked nor protected.

statement: Equipment and media holding data are checked, and data and licensed software are wiped or destroyed by an approved method, before disposal or reuse. Each wipe or destruction is verified, and wipe reports, destruction certificates or a disposal log are kept against the asset record.
why_asked: Disposed or reissued devices often still hold readable data, and a wipe nobody verified is no better than none.
how_to_ask: Ask who wipes devices, by what method and who checks. Ask for the last disposal batch records. Example probe: "Take a laptop retired last quarter and show me the wipe report and where it left the building."
question: Does your organization verify, with proof, that equipment and media holding data are wiped or destroyed before disposal or reuse?
expected_evidence: Equipment disposal and reuse procedure; wipe reports; destruction certificates; disposal log tied to asset inventory entries; disposal contractor agreement. Cover the audit period.
good_looks_like: A procedure requires check and wipe or destruction before disposal or reuse. Each disposed or reissued device has a verified wipe report or certificate linked to its asset record.
test: Sample disposed or reissued devices and media from the audit period. Check each has a wipe report or destruction certificate and a matching asset record. Pass if all sampled devices have verified proof of sanitization.
baseline_risk: Data is recovered from discarded or reused equipment, exposing information to whoever receives it.
